title: Maga-tsuki
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Yasuke, a high-school boy whose family keeps a Shinto shrine, breaks the shrine's sacred mirror just before confessing to his childhood friend Akari, releasing Orihime, a goddess of misfortune who takes his soul. He must stay close to her or die, and can be revived only by her kiss. Further goddesses, including the sun goddess Amaterasu and a fox god, fall for him in a harem comedy that ends with a joint marriage.
life_message: Kindness that makes a lonely goddess happy is rewarded, and everyone who loves Yasuke ends up living together as one household.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Conflicts resolved by making Orihime happy, not by force (Wikipedia).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Curses bind Yasuke, but the household chooses its own unusual arrangement.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Shrine family, fiancee cousin and a shared household (Wikipedia).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Yasuke inherits the role of head priest; gods outrank humans (Wikipedia).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Shinto shrine, kami and purification guide the plot (Wikipedia).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Happiness of others matters more than security.

folkways.japan: Shrine-family succession, the sacred mirror and kami such as Amaterasu come from Shinto, and the cheerful mix of deities with everyday school life is common in Japanese popular culture.

delivery.evidence: AIPT review calls it a formulaic harem comedy with almost no plot; no message identified.
delivery.note: Sources describe light harem comedy with no argued viewpoint.

winners_losers: Everyone wins: Orihime is purified and all heroines marry Yasuke. Sympathy goes to the lonely goddesses.
